title: Lav 1
hookLine: the first round: take up the work of dharma and the Name (Suhi M4, ang 773)

lines: A MORNING WEDDING IN A GURDWARA.
cards: It's early morning at a gurdwara, and the hall is full of bright clothes.

The bride and groom sit side by side on the floor, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, with a long scarf joining them, his end on his shoulder, hers in her hand. The hall goes quiet as the granthi turns to the page.
The couple doesn't write vows. The words that marry them are a Guru's, and they come in four rounds.

teach.h: ANAND KARAJ: THE CEREMONY OF BLISS.
teach.b: This is the Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss. At its center are four stanzas by Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, in Raag Suhi, on Ang seven seventy-three. Each stanza is a lav, a round; together they're the laavan.
The granthi reads the first stanza aloud.
Then the ragis sing it, and while they sing, the couple walks once around the Guru Granth Sahib, clockwise, the groom usually a step ahead, the bride holding her end of the scarf.
They bow, sit, and the next stanza is read. Four readings, four songs, four walks. The first round says, in paraphrase: in the first round, the Lord sets out the work of the householder's life.

Take the Guru's word as your scripture; hold to dharma, right living; remember the Name. Notice what's missing: romance, the families, the future house. It talks about a way of life the two will now walk together.
Sikh teachers often read the four rounds on two levels at once: a husband and wife beginning a shared life, and a soul beginning its journey toward God.

teach.h: ROUND ONE: DUTY, THE WORD, THE NAME.
teach.b: Round one is where both start: ordinary duty, done with the Name in mind.
Guru Ram Das wrote it as a householder himself, a married man with children.
In Sikh teaching that matters: the spiritual life isn't found by running away from home, but walked right through it.

how: At an Anand Karaj, the granthi reads each of Guru Ram Das's four laavan stanzas, then the ragis sing it while the couple walks clockwise around the Guru Granth Sahib; the first round speaks of dharma and the Name.

o: the scarf that joins the couple
one round of the Sikh wedding

games.q: the granthi has just read the first stanza aloud. what happens next?
o: the ragis sing it while the couple walks once around the Guru Granth Sahib.
games.why: the stanza is sung as the couple walks a clockwise circle, then they bow and sit for the next round.

practice: If you have room, stand and walk one slow circle, clockwise, around a chair, a table or a spot on the floor; if you can't walk, trace a circle with your hand.

As you go, hold one plain duty in your life, the dishes, a shift at work, a call to a parent, and let it be part of the circle, not an interruption to it. If you pray, say Waheguru as you finish the round.
